scribe_response.text: Tell me about your first job. My first job began on a wet Monday in September nineteen sixty-seven, when I um was nineteen. I arrived at Saint Aldric's Infirmary in Leeds with a suitcase and a stomach full of knots. The nurses' home stood behind uh the main building, a red brick barrack with long cold corridors. I shared a room with a girl called Maureen Flaherty, who snored and sang in her sleep. Our uniform was a blue striped dress, a white apron, black stockings and a starched cap. The cap took half an hour to fold, and mine collapsed in front of Matron on the first day. Matron Fairweather was um a tall woman with a face like a closed book. She looked at my cap and said that a nurse who cannot fold linen cannot be trusted with people. Nobody had warned me that nursing began with laundry, bedpans um and scrubbing floors. For three months I swept, polished and carried, and I was not allowed near a patient's pulse. Sister Cartwright, who ran my first ward, taught me to make a bed with hospital corners. She pulled the sheet apart each time I finished and told me to begin again. By the fifth try I wanted to throw the uh sheet in her face, but I made it perfect. What happened next? She nodded once, which was the highest praise she had um in her. In the evenings we studied anatomy from a big grey book and learned the bones by heart. Our lessons were in a damp classroom with a skeleton called Percy. Early in my training, a retired carpenter named Mister Arkwright came onto the ward with pneumonia. He spent weeks coughing and whittling, and he never told me what he was making. On my twentieth birthday he pressed uh a tiny wooden sparrow into my hand, um carved from an offcut of a bed-slat. I still um keep it on my kitchen windowsill, and I touch it every morning when I fill the kettle. After that first year, I was finally allowed to take temperatures and um pulses. I remember my first real patient, a man with a broken leg who taught me to play cribbage. He cheated shamelessly, and I let him, because it kept him cheerful. Night duty was the hardest, with a lamp on the uh desk and long shadows down the ward. I walked the ward every hour, listening to breathing. I learned to tell by the sound um of a cough how a night would go. Can you tell me more about that? The first time somebody died on my watch, I was twenty and I stood frozen at the bedside. An older nurse called Gwen put her arm round me and said that we do this for the living, too. I went into the uh sluice room and cried into a bundle of towels. Then uh I washed my face, tidied my cap and went back to work. Our pay was thirty-one, was thirty-one pounds a month, and half of it went on stockings and bus fares. Sometimes we crept out of the nurses' home over the wall to go dancing at the Mecca. We came back at midnight with our shoes in our hands, and Matron always seemed to know. She never mentioned it, but I noticed a lot more scrubbing duty the next morning. We were young, tired and cheerful, and we thought we were saving the world. In a small way, perhaps we were, one bed and one sheet at a time. I qualified in nineteen seventy, and my parents came to the ceremony in their best coats. My mother wept into her handkerchief, and my father shook hands with Matron. I received a silver badge and a certificate in a dark green folder. It was a hard beginning, but I knew by the end of that first winter that I had found my work.
